record.paper_title: Trimer Covers in the Triangular Grid: Twenty Mostly Open Problems
record.context_brief: left stones two bones offset formula
record.original_question: Let T012(a,b) denote the number of tilings of the (a,b)-benzel in which left stones are allowed, right stones are forbidden, and exactly two of the three bone orientations are allowed. Is it true that T012(3n+1, 3n+2) = 2^n n! for every n >= 1?

evidence.quote: For 0 <= i, j <= 1 and 0 <= k <= 3 we define Tijk (a, b) as the number of ways to tile the (a, b)-benzel if the set of allowed prototiles contains the right stone iff i = 1, contains the left stone iff j = 1, and contains k of the bones. We say that such a tiling is an i, j, k tiling.
Problem 3: Is it true that T012 (3n + 1, 3n + 2) = 2^n n! for n >= 1?
Comment: Colin Defant, Rupert Li, Benjamin Young and I worked on problem 2 during the conference and later succeeded in solving Problems 2 and 3; see [3].

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the triangular grid and the hexagonal (honeycomb) lattice dual to it. For positive integers $a,b$, the $(a,b)$-benzel is a specific finite region of the hexagonal grid (a hexagonal analogue of the Aztec diamond) whose precise definition is the following: take all hexagonal cells whose centers $(x,y)$ satisfy the four inequalities $b \le 2x+y$, $2x+y \le 2a+b-1$, $-a \le x-y \le a+b-1$ (after a suitable normalization of axes). The prototiles considered here are "trihexes" (connected unions of three hexagonal cells), grouped into two classes:
- Stones: a "left stone" and a "right stone" (the two mirror-image triangular arrangements of three hexagons meeting at a vertex);
- Bones: three straight trihexes obtained by gluing three hexagons in a row, occurring in three possible orientations (vertical, rising, and falling).

For $i,j \in \{0,1\}$ and $k \in \{0,1,2,3\}$, let $T_{ijk}(a,b)$ denote the number of tilings of the $(a,b)$-benzel by translates of the prototiles, where the right stone is allowed iff $i=1$, the left stone is allowed iff $j=1$, and exactly $k$ of the three bone orientations are allowed (when $k=2$, the count is summed/considered over the relevant choice of which two bone orientations are permitted, in accordance with the standard convention that makes $T_{ijk}$ well-defined as in the formulation of the conjecture).

Prove or disprove: for every integer $n \ge 1$,
$$T_{012}(3n+1,\,3n+2) \;=\; 2^n\, n!.$$
artifact.status_search_result: The conjecture was resolved by Defant, Li, Propp, and Young, who proved several of Propp's enumerative benzel-tiling conjectures (including this one) using a bijection called compression between ribbon tilings, and later via a generalized compression argument.

status_evidence.title: Tilings of Benzels via the Abacus Bijection
status_evidence.snippet: Defant, Li, Propp, and Young recently resolved two enumerative conjectures of Propp concerning the tilings of benzels.
status_evidence.claim: Two of Propp's benzel-tiling conjectures (including Problem 3) were resolved.

status_evidence.title: Tilings of Benzels via Generalized Compression
status_evidence.snippet: We present a generalized version of compression ... using this strengthened tool to resolve three more of Propp's conjectures.
status_evidence.claim: Further Propp benzel conjectures were resolved via generalized compression.
